Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Keep the supplied language.", "input": "Greenhouse watering rota

The rota covers the east and west houses at Bellmere Community Greenhouse, where six volunteers share the morning watering work from Monday through Saturday. The doors open at 7:30, and the first person on duty signs the clipboard beside the potting bench before turning on any valves. Sunday is reserved for inspection rather than routine watering. The rota is posted on the noticeboard by the entrance and copied into the shared calendar, so a volunteer can check the week without relying on a message from the previous person.

Each shift usually takes between forty and fifty minutes. The east house contains the seedling tables, the herb bench, and the row of young citrus trees; the west house holds tomatoes, peppers, and the larger pots of overwintered plants. The labels on the benches use the same letters as the watering map. Volunteers carry a blue can for seedlings and a green can for pots that are not connected to the drip line. The two cans have different rose heads, and both are stored upside down to keep dust out.

The first volunteer checks the rain gauge and the moisture meter before deciding which zones need water. The meter is useful, but it does not replace a look at the compost: a dry surface can cover damp soil below, especially after a cool night. The seedling trays are checked at the corners as well as in the middle because the outer cells dry first. If the leaves are already wet from condensation, the volunteer waters the compost carefully rather than spraying the foliage. A short note on the clipboard records which zones were watered and which were left for another check.

The rota has a few practical rules that prevent one shift from undoing the work of another. Water is applied slowly, with a pause between passes, so it can soak into the pots instead of running across the bench. The drip line is turned on only after the filter has been checked for grit, and it is turned off at the tap rather than by pulling the tubing. Seedlings get small amounts more often; established citrus trees get a deeper soak when the soil is dry several centimetres down. No one adds feed during a watering shift, since feed days are marked separately on the calendar.

1. Monday: Nia checks the seedling trays in the east house and waters the herb bench if the compost is dry below the surface. She also empties the rain gauge and writes the reading on the clipboard.
2. Tuesday: Omar inspects the west-house drip line, cleans its filter if needed, and waters the tomato and pepper pots that are not receiving enough from the line.
3. Wednesday: Lena covers both houses, with extra attention to the young citrus trees. She notes any leaves with curled edges and leaves the pots alone if their lower compost is still damp.
4. Thursday: Peter checks the seedling corners and the larger west-house pots. He compares the moisture meter reading with the compost before choosing whether to use the blue or green can.
5. Friday and Saturday: Mei and Rowan take one day each, in that order. They check the previous notes, water only the zones that need it, and leave a clear entry for whoever comes next.

The schedule changes when someone is away, but swaps are written on the clipboard and entered in the shared calendar before the shift starts. A volunteer who cannot make a morning should contact the next person on the list and agree on a replacement, rather than assuming that the next person will arrive early. Last month, Nia traded her Tuesday for Rowan’s Thursday because of a class, and both dates were changed in the calendar. “I can cover the west house, but I can’t take the whole morning,” Omar said when another swap was proposed, so Lena agreed to handle the east house that day.

A low reading in the cistern changes the order of work. If the water level is below the painted yellow mark, volunteers water the seedling trays and the newly planted citrus first, then check the west-house pots and leave any that remain damp. They do not use the reserve barrel unless the coordinator has confirmed that the cistern valve is working properly. This condition matters most in hot weather, when the cistern can fall quickly and the reserve barrel is also needed for the public planting beds. The person who finds the level below the mark writes the reading and the time beside the day’s entry.

On Saturday afternoon, the coordinator reviews the notes and checks for patterns rather than judging a shift by the amount of water used. A tray that dries out twice in one week may need to be moved away from the warm glass, while a wet corner beneath the west-house bench may point to a leaking joint. Volunteers are asked to report a leak promptly and to put a small tray beneath a slow drip until it can be repaired. The greenhouse keeps spare washers, a filter brush, and two hose connectors in the labelled drawer under the potting bench; tools go back there after use.

The rota is intended to make care predictable without making volunteers follow it blindly. Weather, plant size, and the condition of the compost can change what a particular shift needs to do, so the written notes explain decisions as well as actions. When a zone is deliberately left dry, the volunteer records that choice and the reason, such as damp lower soil or a recent rain. If the cistern is below the yellow mark, the seedling and newly planted citrus priorities still apply even when the usual shift holder is away. At the end of each shift, the tap is closed, the cans are returned to their hooks, and the clipboard is left open to the next blank line.", "output": "Greenhouse watering rota
